examples.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2 = 20.$
examples.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/31f8c54fecdb8b2e8b3f3cad20a642a39eab9ae2987d49849a1c1dabc34e5368.png)

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 20
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=20 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=10.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_2=20,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}19 & -3 \\ -3 & 11\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/51897cac20d424f599eba1c8aada5259279ab9ad263e7557d6614ce79e68fa0f.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/f9913f9139af447be912bccc2350f086ce32bae89849495f8e82a3eebf8a7918.png)

- For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}19 & -3 \\ -3 & 11\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/2cdd8527be173b17e254bd4ecda571d71b15938c3a1f6cb2609122db2b10c64d.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/f6764ef3200afce932740e8100915018b6a0c21e902d932b218e79bcd57e0b95.png)

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/1549a73afb90f3fa0fb8218d9d63daa1a5534c3e546613cbf3f226371b8f1092.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/d4a6e3f0c138e6dd83252df8adc14359ba67ae77dec0270264ea6d00c7b08667.png)

feedback.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-7)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-7)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
